claims.text: Short-time spark plasma infiltration followed by low-temperature annealing will increase copper-phase continuity in W–Cu composites.
The staged process will increase the thermal conductivity of W–Cu composites.
The staged process will retain the mechanical durability of the tungsten matrix under fusion-reactor joint conditions.
The staged process will retain irradiation resistance under fusion-reactor joint conditions.
Conventionally processed W–Cu composites have modest copper connectivity, residual porosity, and less-optimized W–Cu interfaces.
Short-duration spark plasma infiltration rapidly densifies W–Cu composites.
Low-temperature annealing improves W–Cu interfacial bonding.
Low-temperature annealing minimizes porosity in the infiltrated W–Cu composite.
Reduced porosity and optimized W–Cu interfaces improve electron and phonon transport.
A continuous copper phase is crucial for heat conduction in W–Cu composites.
Improved interfacial bonding and fewer defects reduce electron and phonon scattering centers.
Reducing electron and phonon scattering boosts thermal conductivity.
The tungsten backbone provides robust mechanical integrity and inherent irradiation resistance.
Limiting defect propagation allows the tungsten backbone to retain mechanical integrity and irradiation resistance.
The staged composite will maintain or slightly enhance mechanical durability relative to conventionally processed W–Cu composites.
The staged composite will maintain or slightly enhance irradiation resistance relative to conventionally processed W–Cu composites.
Conventional melt infiltration or sintering produces lower copper connectivity and greater porosity that limit thermal conduction and may compromise irradiation performance.
Excessively high annealing temperatures or prolonged dwell times could cause unwanted intermetallic formation or phase coarsening that negates the benefits.
